title: Toric codes all the way down: decoupling translation-invariant topological CSS codes in higher dimensions
authors: Mingxin He, Yifei Wang, Hao Song, Yingfei Gu
abstract: Topological Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes in more than two spatial dimensions offer features useful for fault-tolerant quantum computation, such as transversal non-Clifford gates and single-shot decoding, but a systematic understanding of them is still lacking. One approach is to decouple a code: map it to a stack of higher-form toric codes by a finite-depth local CSS-preserving Clifford circuit, possibly after adding ancillas. For translation-invariant $p$-ary CSS codes, where $p$ is prime ($p=2$ for qubits), we require the circuit to commute with the translations of a superlattice. In two dimensions, such a decoupling exists once these translations act trivially on every anyon type. In higher dimensions, excitations are sorted by their dimension into superselection layers, which can remain glued together even when translations act trivially on each layer. We show that this gluing is the only remaining obstruction: a code can be decoupled on a superlattice exactly when, after coarse-graining to it, translations act trivially on every layer and the gluing vanishes. Moreover, for a code with finitely many excitation types in each layer and $m$ nonzero layers, once translations act trivially on every layer, further coarse-graining by a factor of $p^{m-1}$ in every direction removes the aforementioned gluing. Physically, the same criterion determines when the code encodes the maximal number of logical qudits on a finite torus. Finally, we give an explicit algorithm that constructs the decoupling as a circuit of SUM (qudit CNOT) and SWAP gates.
summary: This paper develops a rigorous mathematical criterion to determine when higher-dimensional, translation-invariant topological CSS codes can be simplified or 'decoupled' into a stack of simpler toric codes. The key finding is that the primary obstruction to this decoupling is a structural 'gluing' between excitation layers, which can be removed via coarse-graining. This provides a powerful tool for analyzing the true logical capacity of quantum memory architectures.
main_problem: The paper addresses the systematic understanding and conditions for decoupling translation-invariant topological Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes in higher dimensions ($D \ge 3$).
main_result: Decoupling is possible if and only if, after coarse-graining, translations act trivially on every excitation layer and the 'gluing' between these layers vanishes.
method: The analysis uses algebraic methods involving Laurent polynomial rings and module theory to compare the code complex with the stack complex of higher-form toric codes.
model_or_system: The system is topological CSS codes defined on a superlattice ($\mathbb{Z}^D$) using $p$-ary qudits, which are compared against the structure of higher-form toric codes.
key_observables: The superselection profile, which describes how excitation layers are 'glued together', and the number of logical qudits encoded on a torus.
important_parameters: The spatial dimension $D$, the prime $p$ defining the qudits, and the lattice structure (superlattice/torus).
main_assumptions: The code is assumed to have finitely many excitation types in each layer, and the analysis relies on algebraic machinery involving module resolutions and coarse-graining procedures.

paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by establishing algebraic criteria for decoupling, identifying the 'gluing' as the primary obstruction, and concluding with an explicit algorithm for constructing the necessary Clifford circuit.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous mathematical criteria for understanding the fault-tolerance capabilities of complex quantum codes in higher dimensions, which is fundamental to quantum computation theory.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Three-dimensional toric codes. (a) TC(3) 1 (Fp), with qudits on edges. (b) TC(3) 2 (Fp), with qudits on plaquettes. The right panels show local relations among the checks; in each oriented product, every qudit involved is acted on by exactly two of the checks, with opposite exponents. In all figures, blue refers to TC(3) 1 (Fp) and orange to TC(3) 2 (Fp); stars mark X-type checks and diamonds Z-type checks, and colored edges and plaquettes mark qudits.

FIG. 3. Why the charge cannot be detached from the loop on the original lattice (x1x2-plane, both codes superposed; open stars mark checks no longer violated). (a) Z on a plaquette creates a loop and the charge −1 at its corner. (b) An at- tached string moves the charge but preserves the total. (c) A new check: the X-type check of TC(3) 1 (Fp) at a vertex times a power of that of TC(3) 2 (Fp) on the x1-edge above it. (d) With every vertex relabeled, the top edge of a plaquette removes the charge at its corner, but the bottom edge creates it at the vertex below.
